stories.title: AmTrustRE Brings Financial District Office Tower to 100% Occupancy
stories.excerpt: AmTrustRE, a national real estate owner-operator, said Tuesday that 59 Maiden Ln., its 1,043,670-square-foot office tower in Manhattan’s Financial District, has reached 100% occupancy. The leasing milestone occurs with a new, 14,807-square-foot lease with Blackstone-backed ANV Group Holdings Ltd. and a 58,164-square-foot renewal from London Fischer LLP. The full occupancy comes ahead of the completion of the property’s extensive repositioning, including its facade and lobby renovations expected in 2027, and a redesigned public plaza, slated for completion later this year. “Reaching full occupancy before completing the transformation of 59 Maiden Ln. is a meaningful validation of our long-term investment strategy,“ said Jonathan Bennett, President of AmTrustRE. “By thoughtfully repositioning an exceptionally well-located asset and reinvesting in the building and tenant experience, we’ve created a workplace that drives strong leasing outcomes and competes with the best assets in the market.” ANV and AmTrustRE were both self-represented in the new lease. Bud London, Managing Partner of London Fischer, represented the firm in the renewal, while AmTrustRE was self-represented by Anne Holker, Managing Director Leasing and Acquisitions of AmTrustRE. The post AmTrustRE Brings Financial District Office Tower to 100% Occupancy appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.summary: AmTrustRE's 59 Maiden Ln. in Manhattan's Financial District reached 100% occupancy ahead of completion of its extensive facade and lobby renovations (expected 2027) and public plaza redesign. The milestone came via a new 14,807-square-foot lease with ANV Group Holdings Ltd. (Blackstone-backed) and a 58,164-square-foot renewal from London Fischer LLP. Management framed full occupancy as validation of its long-term repositioning strategy.

Office stabilization in Manhattan's Financial District reflects broader demand for repositioned legacy stock, but does not signal residential supply pressures or rental demand shifts. No implications for apartment development pipeline or market dynamics in Manhattan or other major metros.

stories.title: CBRE Arranges 118K-SF Price Zone Lease in Commerce
stories.excerpt: CBRE arranged a nearly 118,000-square-foot industrial lease at Harris Business Center in Commerce to Price Zone, a wholesale distributor and importer of consumer goods. The transaction allows Price Zone to consolidate operations previously spread among three separate facilities. CBRE’s Cameron Merrill and Jeff Stephens represented the landlord, DWS. The tenant was represented by John Lee of Curb Realty. “Price Zone’s primary objective was operational consolidation, and 6000 Rickenbacker Rd. provided an attractive opportunity to achieve that goal,” said Merrill. “The transaction delivered the efficiency and economics the tenant was seeking while helping ownership maximize occupancy within the business park. The result was a solution that closely aligned with each party’s long-term objectives.” The facility is located at 6000-6050 Rickenbacker Rd. and features a 24-foot clearance in the warehouse, along with 19 dock-high loading positions and three ground-level doors. It also has rail service provided by the Los Angeles Junction Railway. The post CBRE Arranges 118K-SF Price Zone Lease in Commerce appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Price Zone leases 118,000-SF industrial facility in Commerce (Harris Business Center, 6000 Rickenbacker Rd.)
Consolidation of three separate facilities into single 24-foot-clearance warehouse with rail access
Strong LA industrial leasing activity supports continued logistics/distribution cluster near ports
stories.summary: CBRE arranged a 117,700-square-foot industrial lease at Harris Business Center in Commerce for Price Zone, a wholesale distributor consolidating operations from three separate facilities into a single location. The facility at 6000 Rickenbacker Rd. features 24-foot clearance, 19 dock-high loading positions, three ground-level doors, and rail service via Los Angeles Junction Railway. The transaction aligned operational and economic efficiency for both tenant and landlord DWS.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. Industrial consolidation in Commerce reflects port-adjacent logistics market strength, not residential demand signals. No secondary effects on apartment supply, financing, or market fundamentals in Southern California or other key metros.

stories.title: Terreno Adds to NYC Portfolio with Red Hook Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Terreno Realty Corporation, a Bellevue, WA-based owner and operator of industrial real estate, acquired an industrial property located in Red Hook Brooklyn, for approximately $26.3 million. The seller was not identified. Located at 659 Court St., the property consists of one industrial distribution building containing approximately 28,000 square feet on 1.5 acres. It provides two grade-level loading positions and parking for 70 cars. The property has riparian access and is 100% leased to a maritime goods and services provider. The estimated stabilized cap rate is 5.2%. Terreno acquires, owns and operates industrial real estate in six major coastal U.S. markets: New York City/Northern New Jersey, Los Angeles, Miami, San Francisco Bay Area, Seattle and Washington, DC. Its NYC/NJ portfolio now encompasses 69 properties totaling nearly 3.6 million square feet, making it the largest by building count among the six markets. The post Terreno Adds to NYC Portfolio with Red Hook Acquisition appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Terreno Realty acquires 28,000-SF Red Hook Brooklyn industrial property for $26.3M (5.2% cap rate)

The property is 100% leased to a maritime goods and services provider, offers two grade-level loading positions and 70 parking spaces, and has riparian access. The stabilized cap rate is 5.2%. Terreno's NYC/NJ portfolio now encompasses 69 properties totaling nearly 3.6 million square feet, making it the largest by building count in the company's six-market coastal footprint.

Red Hook industrial consolidation does not materially shift residential supply, demand, or financing conditions in Brooklyn or NYC submarkets. Industrial and residential CRE cycles operate separately; no material cross-market effect.

stories.title: Building Block Foundation Fund: CRE Industry’s Way to Make a Difference
stories.excerpt: Presented by Bob O’Neill, executive vice president, CapRock Partners, Building Block Foundation Fund Boardmember. CapRock is also Endless Summer Title Sponsor. Why should people get involved with Building Block Foundation Fund? Building Block Foundation Fund is a nonprofit organized by volunteer professionals from across the commercial real estate industry. Our fundraising efforts involve bringing people together to network and spend time with their CRE peers – which makes Building Block unique. There are several Orange County charities with compelling missions, and they draw from supporters from across the entire Southern California and Orange County business and corporate spectrum, so those charity event attendees are not necessarily building business connections with people focused in their industry. We are 100% commercial real estate focused, which is a key reason why CRE industry people should support Building Block. What inspired your involvement with Building Block Foundation Fund? I had a friend who was on the board who invited me to get involved. While I was considering joining the board, three thoughts came to mind: I have an extensive business network, I’m not afraid to ask the question of people to support our mission, and I knew I could make a difference in the communities and charities that we donate to. It also matters to CapRock Partners because one of our seven core values is ‘Blessed to be a Blessing.” Our principals set aside 10% of partner profits to reinvest in the communities where we invest and develop. Building Block is an important part of that goal. How does Building Block choose its charities? There’s a great deal of need in Orange County. Everywhere you look, there are multiple charities doing great work, but unfortunately, we can’t support all of them. bullets: Building Block Foundation Fund nonprofit fundraising initiative led by CRE industry volunteers
CapRock Partners executive Bob O'Neill highlights peer networking and philanthropic mission
No bearing on market dynamics, supply, demand, capital, or construction costs

stories.title: Prism Partners Trades Two-Building Edison Lofts for $131M
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield arranged the $131-million investment sale of Edison Lofts, a 334-unit luxury multifamily community with nearly 19,000 square feet of retail space at 33 Ashland Ave. in West Orange, NJ. The Cushman & Wakefield team of Niko Nicolaou, Ryan Dowd, JP Hohl, Michael Guerra, Kelly Kellett and Alexandria Russo Ebers represented both the seller, Prism Partners and its capital partners, and the buyer, Sym Investments. Cushman & Wakefield’s Equity, Debt & Structured Finance team of John Alascio, Brad Domenico, and Chuck Kohaut arranged a $91.7-million acquisition loan featuring a full-term interest-only structure from New York Life. “Edison Lofts attracted significant investor interest because it offers a combination that is increasingly difficult to replicate in today’s market,” said Nicolaou. “The property delivers the character of a historic conversion with the scale, amenities and accessibility that continue to resonate with today’s renters. Coupled with strong occupancy and a favorable tax pilot, it represented a rare opportunity to acquire a well-positioned multifamily asset in one of Northern New Jersey’s most active investment markets.” Edison Lofts comprises two residential buildings totaling 334 apartments. The community includes The Residences at Edison Lofts, a 300-unit conversion of the historic Thomas Edison Battery Building, a former manufacturing building, and The Mews at Edison Lofts, a 34-unit ground-up residential building. The post Prism Partners Trades Two-Building Edison Lofts for $131M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Prism Partners sells 334-unit Edison Lofts (West Orange, NJ) for $131M to Sym Investments
19,000-SF retail; strong occupancy and favorable tax PILOT; $91.7M acquisition loan from New York Life (IO structure)
Historic conversion with scale and accessibility in active Northern NJ submarket commands investor appetite
stories.summary: Cushman & Wakefield arranged the $131 million investment sale of Edison Lofts, a 334-unit luxury multifamily community at 33 Ashland Ave. in West Orange, NJ, from seller Prism Partners to buyer Sym Investments. The property includes nearly 19,000 square feet of retail space. The sale closed with a $91.7 million acquisition loan from New York Life featuring a full-term interest-only structure. The property's character as a historic conversion combined with strong occupancy, amenity quality, and a favorable tax PILOT attracted significant investor interest in Northern Jersey's active multifamily market.
stories.impact: Edison Lofts sale demonstrates continued institutional appetite for well-stabilized, value-add multifamily assets in Northern Jersey suburbs, particularly historic conversions with retail. Tax abatement (PILOT) and IO debt structure reflect competitive cap rates (~4–5%) and sustained liquidity for stabilized assets near NYC. No signal of new supply pressure or development feasibility shift; market remains favorable for quality infill acquisitions but signals tightening yields relative to prior cycles.

stories.title: OCVibe’s Scott Frick On Building a $5B District Around Anaheim’s Honda Center
stories.excerpt: A 100-acre master-planned development is turning the sea of parking lots surrounding Anaheim’s Honda Center into a dense mixed-use district where people can live, work and eat whether or not the Ducks are playing. Henry and Susan Samueli, owners of the National Hockey League’s Anaheim Ducks, are privately financing the large development named OCVibe. Scott Frick, senior vice president of real estate and district operations at the Samueli’s Orange County Sports & Entertainment, is managing the project, and described it as a $5 billion investment with 170,000 square feet of office space, more than 2,000 apartments, two hotels and more than 35 dining concepts. The broader plan also includes 20 acres of parks and plazas. The first major public-facing pieces are scheduled to arrive in 2027, including Katella Commons, a 50,000-square-foot market hall, along with a 5,000-capacity concert venue, and The Weave, a six-story mass-timber office building where flexible-office operator Kiln has committed to a full floor. Then the Honda Center will host indoor volleyball during the 2028 Olympics, when Frick expects roughly half a million people to pass through the arena in 11 days. Commercial Observer spoke with Frick about how the absence of outside investors changes the economics, OCVibe’s office and residential strategy, and how to keep restaurants busy when the arena goes dark. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.   Commercial Observer: Can you give an overview of where construction stands today? Scott Frick: We started construction about three years ago. We’ll be delivering phases through about 2030, 2031. The first phase was really building parking structures to free up the surface lots. Honda Center is a very typical suburban arena. It’s kind of in the middle of nowhere, surrounded by surface parking and industrial uses. Over the last eight years, we’ve assembled almost 10 different parcels to create the 100-acre footprint. Parking decks were de
bullets: OCVibe: 100-acre $5B master-planned district around Anaheim Honda Center (Ducks ownership, Samueli family)
2,000+ apartments, 170,000-SF office, 2 hotels, 35+ dining venues; first delivery 2027 (Katella Commons, concert venue, Kiln office)
Private equity-backed transformation of parking-lot submarket into mixed-use destination; 20 acres parks/plazas
stories.summary: OCVibe, a $5 billion privately financed master-planned development by Anaheim Ducks owners Henry and Susan Samueli, will transform 100 acres of parking lots surrounding Honda Center into a dense mixed-use district. The project includes more than 2,000 apartments, 170,000 square feet of office space, two hotels, and more than 35 dining concepts, plus 20 acres of parks and plazas. First major components, including Katella Commons (50,000-SF market hall), a 5,000-capacity concert venue, and The Weave (six-story mass-timber office with Kiln flexible workspace), are scheduled for 2027. The project is managed by Scott Frick, SVP of real estate and district operations at Orange County Sports & Entertainment.
stories.impact: Significant supply catalyst for Orange County/Anaheim submarket post-2027. Delivery of 2,000+ units into Anaheim will increase regional multifamily stock and potentially compress rents in Orange County if absorption lags. However, OCVibe's integrated entertainment/dining/office ecosystem positions it as destination product likely to capture new demand rather than cannibalize existing stock. Developer interest in mass-timber office suggests feasibility of premium, sustainable product. Primary risk: timing sensitivity to market conditions in 2027–2029; if cap rates compress further or debt becomes unavailable, construction pace may slow, delaying supply impact.

stories.title: Pinnacle Group Sells Rights to Upper West Side Apartment Tower for $88M
stories.excerpt: Pinnacle Group has offloaded another asset, this time on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. The prominent New York City landlord, which put a massive rent-stabilized portfolio into bankruptcy last year, sold its rights to an apartment building at 323 West 96th Street to private real estate company Lightstone Group for approximately $88 million, according to a source with knowledge of the deal. The Real Deal first reported the sale, citing filings by Pinnacle’s parent company, Zarasai Group, with the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange. The filings, dated Aug. 13, announced the successfully completed sale of Pinnacle’s 100 percent interest in the 15-story building’s lease rights and a 50 percent hold on the land rights. Daniel Parker, Gary Phillips and Will Silverman at Eastdil Secured Savills advised on the deal. An $11 million surplus from the sale is slated to be deposited into the account of Series C bondholders. A spokesperson for Pinnacle Group could not be reached for comment on the most recent sale. The property carried an existing loan balance of about $65 million as of late March, last transferred from Starwood Mortgage Capital to a Barclays-sponsored commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) trust in 2023. Pinnacle secured the leasehold to 323 West 96th Street in 2007, according to city records, and paid another $27 million for its land rights stake in 2016. The 173-unit apartment building, built in 2001, sits at the corner of East 96th Street and First Avenue. The sale comes days after news that Pinnacle offloaded a $128 million condominium and commercial portfolio spanning 39 transactions across Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan. The buyer was Friar Park JW, an entity with links to Tremada Holdings, an affiliate of London-based property company William Pears Group. Pinnacle, led by Joel Wiener, placed a portfolio of roughly 5,000 rent-stabilized apartments across New York City into bankruptcy in May 2025 after facing approximately $574.4 million in debt. stories.summary: Pinnacle Group sold its 100% interest in lease rights and 50% of land rights to the 15-story apartment building at 323 West 96th Street on Manhattan's Upper West Side to private real estate company Lightstone Group for approximately $88 million. The transaction was announced via Zarasai Group (Pinnacle's parent) filings with the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange. An $11 million surplus from the sale was directed to Series C bondholders after paying off an existing $65 million loan. Eastdil Secured Savills represented the deal.
stories.impact: Reflects ongoing Pinnacle distress liquidation of rent-stabilized Manhattan portfolio (filed bankruptcy ~1 year prior). Lightstone acquisition of Upper West Side rent-stabilized asset signals institutional interest in stabilized stabilized in-place cash flows despite regulatory headwinds. Rising number of distress sales of stabilized inventory may pressure cap rates and create acquisition opportunities for well-capitalized buyers, but does NOT increase new multifamily supply. Key monitoring point: if Pinnacle accelerates sales, could release significant stabilized stock into secondary market, affecting valuations for market-rate developers in Manhattan.

stories.title: At New York City Council Hearing on Pied-à-Terre Tax, Complaints of a Sloppy Rollout
stories.excerpt: As a legal battle over New York’s pied-à-terre tax continues, the New York City Council held a hearing Tuesday evaluating the surcharge on second homes. Manhattan Councilmember Gale Brewer led the inquiry against what she saw as a dysfunctional rollout of the tax that included publishing up to 900,000 names and addresses of possible second homes in the five boroughs. The Mamdani administration did not send any representatives to the hearing at City Hall, including from the Department of Finance tasked with collecting the tax. The hearing was held by the Committee on Finance and the Committee on Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation. “No estimate of the number of pied-à-terres in the city comes even close to 900,000,” Brewer said. “Yet, the city still published the list with the small caveat that the properties on the list may be subject to the charge. The list published by the Department of Finance was so overbroad that it even included my name, and I don’t mind my name and my home address [being included], but I’ve been in that home 365 days a year since 1994. I don’t leave the city, and I don’t have a second home.” The committee hoped to get answers from the Mamdani administration on why — when it had credible information from the New York City Comptroller‘s office about how many second homes there are — it still attempted to force thousands of property owners in the city to prove that the addresses are primary residences. Brewer stated that the “onus” should not have been on the homeowners, but on the city to determine whether the home is a primary residence. “Homeowners who believe that they received the letters in error initially had only a short window to contest the surcharge,” Brewer said. “ Although the deadline was ultimately extended by four weeks, this still puts the burden on property owners, which upset people tremendously.” About 17,000 homeowners received letters informing them that they are on the suppl
bullets: NYC Council hearing on pied-à-terre tax; publication of ~900K property names/addresses criticized as overbroad
Mamdani administration (Department of Finance) did not attend hearing; unclear implementation and compliance
Tax design and rollout dysfunction may deter foreign/investor purchases; uncertain revenue collection and market impact
stories.summary: The New York City Council held a hearing Tuesday on the pied-à-terre tax, a surcharge on second homes. Councilmember Gale Brewer criticized the "dysfunctional rollout," highlighting the Department of Finance's publication of approximately 900,000 property names and addresses of suspected second homes—a list Brewer claimed was far too broad and included her own residence. The Mamdani administration did not send representatives to the hearing, raising questions about implementation and enforcement.
stories.impact: Pied-à-terre tax creates headwind for investor acquisitions and foreign capital inflow into Manhattan residential market, reducing demand for new luxury multifamily supply and potentially compressing cap rates if investment volumes decline. However, poor implementation and legal challenges (ongoing litigation) may significantly limit tax collection and deterrent effect. For developers: increased uncertainty around investor buyer pools and pricing; market-rate product targeting owner-occupancy may outperform luxury investment play in Manhattan over next 2–3 years. Monitor legal outcomes and revenue collections to assess true impact on capital flows.

stories.title: Betting on South Beach Luxury Shopping, Vivienne Westwood Plans to Open Store
stories.excerpt: Vivienne Westwood is finally getting serious about opening a boutique in Miami’s South Beach. Almost two years after buying the three-story property at 736 Collins Avenue and letting it sit vacant, the luxury fashion brand has submitted an application to build out the property, which dates back to 1921. The 4,356-square-foot ground-floor space would feature a store with three fittings rooms and two storage rooms. The second floor would house executive offices and meeting rooms, while the top floor would include a bridal showroom and rooftop deck. A neon sign would be mounted onto the entrance wall. The project “honors the building’s 1921 Art Deco and Mediterranean Revival heritage while introducing contemporary elements,” wrote Daniel Gabay, who runs National Permit Group and filed the proposal. The modern elements include “Florida limestone cladding, polished brass storefront and motifs, a rigid canopy reinterpreting the documented historic faux eave, a landmark pink neon signature, and the iconic Orb statue in the forecourt,” per the application, which Miami Beach Historic Preservation Board will consider next month. In 2024, the British brand paid $6 million for the 14,692-square-foot building located just a few blocks west of Ocean Drive, sandwiched between Seventh and Eighth Streets. Unlike most luxury labels of its size, it remains independent under the ownership of Vivienne Westwood’s family. The namesake designer passed away in 2022. Vivienne Westwood, the brand, is betting that high-end retail will return to the heart of South Beach. In the 1990s and 2000s, the area housed boutiques from the likes of Versace, Hugo Boss and Barney’s. But almost all shuttered, opting instead to open outposts at the Bal Harbour Shops up north and the Design District out west, which have become some of the highest-grossing upscale malls in the country. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Vivienne Westwood luxury boutique opening at 736 Collins Avenue, South Beach Miami; vacant ~2 years prior
4,356-SF ground floor retail plus executive/bridal showroom; 1921 Art Deco/Mediterranean Revival renovation
Retail leasing activity suggests South Beach demand recovery for luxury fashion; mixed-use/hospitality confidence
stories.summary: Vivienne Westwood has submitted a construction application for a boutique at 736 Collins Avenue in Miami's South Beach, nearly two years after acquiring the three-story, 1921-vintage property and leaving it vacant. The ground floor will feature a 4,356-square-foot store with three fitting rooms and two storage rooms. The second floor will house executive offices and meeting rooms, while the third floor will include a bridal showroom and rooftop deck. The design honors the building's Art Deco and Mediterranean Revival heritage with contemporary updates including limestone cladding, polished brass, and a landmark pink neon sign.
stories.impact: Luxury retail tenant commitment in South Beach signals confidence in Miami tourism and high-income visitor/resident base, supporting secondary demand for nearby hotels and short-term rental accommodations but NOT primary multifamily rental demand. Does not materially affect apartment development feasibility or demand in Miami, as retail leasing and residential cycles are distinct. Minor positive signal for mixed-use developments anchored by retail/hospitality, but low relevance to multifamily-focused developers.

stories.title: Get to Know the Broker: Vickey Barron of Compass
stories.excerpt: Vickey Barron, an associate broker at Compass, knows how to get deals done — and all with the perfect mix of intelligence, charm, charisma and a take-no-nonsense attitude. It’s what makes her one of the best real estate brokers in the business. Barron, 69, has worked on more than 600 sales during her career and earned a slew of awards, including the Real Estate Board of New York’s Rookie of the Year award in 2001 and the board’s Eileen Spinola Distinguished Service Award in 2015. Barron has done an endless amount of million-dollar deals, but for her, the value of her job isn’t money — it’s the difference she can make in someone’s life. “People always want me to talk about commissions and big sales, and I just am a strong believer that our purpose in this role of real estate is not money and commission and who has the biggest numbers,” Barron said. “It’s really about serving people.” Commercial Observer caught up with Barron in August for a new series called “Get to Know the Broker,” where we connect with residential brokers to learn more about what makes them tick. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What was the biggest deal of your career? Vickey Barron: Ironically, this is not the one with the highest sale price or largest commission. In our business, there tends to be an emphasis on the commissions and money earned, but, going back to basics, we are in the business of helping people find homes and find solace. My biggest and most important deal was helping a 93-year-old woman negotiate a life estate so she could remain in her West Village townhouse after the sale took place. Sometimes we get caught up and forget that we’re all human and we age. Life has chapters, and our contributions matter. This deal had the biggest and most positive impact in my career. At 69, Barron emphasizes client service over commission and views her role as making a difference in people's lives rather than maximizing transaction volume or deal size.
